summary: The note argues that After-Action Reviews (AARs) are central to improving emergency response and building resilience. It uses two 2023 incidents, a 36-hour blackout in New Gotham and a cyber-attack on the Cerberus Power Plant, to show how AARs lead to concrete changes. It also covers the growing role of data analytics, virtual reality, KPIs, cross-organization collaboration and community feedback in future AARs.
one_line: After-Action Reviews of the New Gotham blackout and the Cerberus Power Plant cyber-attack show how lessons, technology, KPIs and community feedback strengthen emergency response.
key_facts: An After-Action Review (AAR) is a structured evaluation after a significant event to analyze what happened, why it happened, and how it can be done better.
On October 10, 2023, a widespread blackout hit New Gotham and lasted 36 hours.
New Gotham's emergency management response to the blackout was led by Coordinator Sarah Jennings, but the scale of the incident left many services strained.
On November 22, 2023, a cyber-attack on the Cerberus Power Plant disrupted electricity supply and exposed cybersecurity vulnerabilities.
Incident commander Michael Chen and his team contained the Cerberus breach, but the damage had already been done.
During the Cerberus attack, local cyber response teams and national security agencies communicated collaboratively, enabling swift containment and a thorough cross-section analysis during the AAR.
New Gotham's Emergency Response Unit, led by Specialist Emily Torres, aims to incorporate Virtual Reality into its AARs, including simulations of past events like the blackout.

Rebecca Clare, Director of the Velocity Disaster Response Agency, saw the blackout review lead to broader protocols for power grid redundancy and faster emergency communications among first responders.
The Cerberus AAR led to enhanced cyber resilience, including improved detection technologies and stronger defense systems.
Post-incident analyses with KPI metrics showed New Gotham response times improved by 18% after lessons learned from previous events were incorporated.
Big data and predictive modeling give planners like Jennings and Chen advanced simulations and 'what-if' analyses to refine emergency responses.
Future AARs are expected to include a broader community feedback loop; community forums and surveys after the recent crises have already provided useful data.
